meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Telegraph is Like a Very, Very Long Cat (or Dog)'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Einstein. The very-long-cat telegraph joke was printed in 1866 with a dog; the cat arrived in 1924, the Einstein credit in 1985.

answer.label: Not Einstein — an anonymous joke first printed in 1866
answer.authorDates: Credited to Albert Einstein (1879–1955) · the joke was in print in 1866, before he was born
answer.sourceLine: No letter, essay, interview or contemporary report puts this line in Einstein’s mouth. Quote Investigator ↗ traces it instead to a joke that circulated anonymously for more than a century: in August 1866 two French peasants explain the telegraph as “an immense long dog” with its head in Vienna and its tail in Paris. The animal became a cat in April 1924, and the punchline “wireless is precisely the same thing without the cat” was already fixed then. Einstein’s name was attached only in 1985.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — a documented 19th-century joke with no author, credited to Einstein a century later.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: None. Nothing connects the remark to Einstein in his lifetime.
August 1866, newspaper filler about two French peasants and “an immense long dog” — head in Vienna, tail in Paris
28 February 1985, in the source code of the Unix fortune program posted to the Usenet group net.sources.games

source.excerpt: You see, wire telegraph is a kind of a very, very long cat. You pull his tail in New York and his head is meowing in Los Angeles. Do you understand this? And radio operates exactly the same way: you send signals here, they receive them there. The only difference is that there is no cat.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ states that “there is no significant evidence that Einstein ever wrote or spoke the passage”, and concludes that the joke “developed over an extended period during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries” among people who were “largely anonymous”.

The 1866 dog anecdote is not hard to check for yourself: it was reprinted that October in The Telegrapher ↗, the journal of the National Telegraphic Union in New York, and again in 1877 in Lightning Flashes and Electric Dashes ↗, an American collection of telegraphic humour, where the dog runs from Brooklyn to Hoboken.

The wireless punchline — the part that makes the Einstein version sound like physics — also predates him in this joke. The Electrical Review ↗ was still printing the plain dog version in December 1914, and QI records a 1917 telling that ends “the dog is imaginary”.

The cat itself is datable. QI credits correspondent Andrew Steinberg with finding the April 1924 instance in the Commercial Telegraphers Journal — “wireless is precisely the same thing without the cat” — and had the page scanned to verify it. Einstein is not mentioned. Wikiquote files the quotation under Misattributed ↗.
source.cutTag: As it circulates under Einstein’s name
source.excerptNote: That is the wording people share. The oldest version anyone has dated is unrecognisably older and has no cat in it: “Imagine that the telegraph is an immense long dog—so long that its head is at Vienna and its tail is at Paris. Well, tread on its tail, which is at Paris, and it will bark at Vienna.” That ran in the Providence Evening Press on 31 August 1866 and in several other American papers the same week.

source.rightsNote: We assert no rights status. The 19th-century tellings are long out of copyright, but the specific wording on this page is not one of them — it is an anonymous 20th-century rewrite whose earliest known appearance is a 1985 Usenet posting, with no identifiable author and no traceable first publication to attach a status to.

author.name: Albert Einstein
author.heading: About Albert Einstein
author.bio: Einstein is the internet’s default signature for any remark that is clever about physics, and this one fits the costume unusually well — it is a good explanation of radio, delivered as a joke, by someone who clearly understands the thing being explained. He did have a gift for exactly this kind of homely analogy, which is part of why the credit stuck. It is still not his: the joke was in American newspapers thirteen years before he was born.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source exists for the Einstein attribution. Earliest documented form of the joke: “A Novel Illustration of the Telegraph,” Providence Evening Press (Providence, RI), 31 August 1866, p. 2, col. 2; reprinted in The Telegrapher (New York: National Telegraphic Union), 15 October 1866, p. 43. Earliest known version featuring a cat: “Headquarters Notes,” Commercial Telegraphers Journal 22, no. 4 (April 1924): 143. Citations as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The joke has been hung on a series of famous names over 160 years. Only one of them is documented as having told a version of it.

items.why: The earliest known Einstein credit is a line of source code in the Unix fortune program distributed on 28 February 1985, which prefaces the text with “Albert Einstein, when asked to describe radio, replied:”. QI found nothing earlier linking him to it ↗, and the joke itself is 119 years older.

A diary entry for 26 July 1873, published in Story of My Life by Augustus Hare in 1901, has Lord Stanhope telling the tale as an explanation given to the visiting Shah — a dog with its tail in London and its head in Teheran. The Shah is the audience in the joke, not its author, and the same anecdote had already been in print for seven years.

items.tag: but a dog, and not this wording
items.why: Wikiquote records ↗ that Edison described being taught the telegraph by “an old Scotch line repairer” using a dachshund long enough to reach from Edinburgh to London. That is Edison repeating the standing joke, not inventing this sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is real, funny and old. It simply has no author — and the trail QI assembled ↗ runs from an 1866 dog to a 1924 cat without passing through Einstein at any point.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Every genuinely new technology arrives needing a metaphor, and the telegraph got a very good one almost immediately. The dog joke works because it smuggles in the one idea people found hardest — that nothing physical travels the wire, that the signal is a disturbance rather than a delivery — and then hands it back as a punchline about treading on a tail.

It survived because it kept upgrading. The dog became a cat; the wire dropped away when wireless arrived; and the closing line, “the same thing without the cat”, turned out to be a serviceable one-sentence account of radio. By 1985 it sounded so much like something a physicist would say that a physicist’s name got attached to it, which is roughly how most Einstein quotations happen.
detailsBody: The 1866 version is set near Paris during the Austro-Prussian war, which was then a few weeks old: one peasant cannot understand how messages travel by wire, and the other reaches for the immense dog. American papers picked it up within days — the Brooklyn Daily Eagle on 28 August, the Providence Evening Press and the Cleveland Leader on 31 August — and the telegraphers’ own trade press ran it that October.

Between then and the 1920s the joke was retold with a rotating cast: the Shah of Persia in 1873 and again in 1894, a pair of American characters connecting Brooklyn and Hoboken in 1877, an “Oriental potentate” in The Electrical Review in 1914. Several of the American tellings are written in a heavy dialect that is unpleasant to read now; QI reproduces them to keep the chain of transmission honest, and the point they establish is simply that the joke was everywhere.

The decisive change is the wireless ending. Once a version existed in which the animal was imaginary, the joke had stopped being about telegraph wires and started being about radio — and that is the version that eventually landed under Einstein’s name.
context.pull: The joke explains radio well enough that people assumed only Einstein could have made it.

sourcesVerified.claim: There is no significant evidence that Einstein ever wrote or spoke the passage; the earliest cite located is a 1985 source code listing of the Unix fortune program distributed 28 February 1985 on net.sources.games.
The earliest instance of the joke QI located is August 1866, featuring a dog with its head at Vienna and its tail at Paris, printed in the Providence Evening Press of 31 August 1866 and other papers.

The first known version featuring a cat rather than a dog is April 1924, Commercial Telegraphers Journal vol. 22 no. 4, p. 143, ending 'wireless is precisely the same thing without the cat'; Einstein is not mentioned.

A diary entry dated 26 July 1873 in Augustus Hare's Story of My Life (published 1901) records Lord Stanhope telling the anecdote about the Shah of Persia and an immense dog between London and Teheran.

Wikiquote lists the very-long-cat quotation in its Misattributed section for Albert Einstein, notes no source in Einstein's original writings has been found, and records Edison's dachshund variant from Edinburgh to London.
The Telegrapher, the journal of the National Telegraphic Union (New York), carries the 1866 long-dog telegraph anecdote.
Lightning Flashes and Electric Dashes (1877), a collection of telegraphic humour, contains an American retelling of the long-dog joke connecting Brooklyn and Hoboken.
The Electrical Review volume 75 (1914) is available in full at the Internet Archive and carries the long-dog explanation of the telegraph.
